messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 33
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Tailor
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 79

He is a 33-year-old African man who works as a tailor, and his life before the attack is organized around steady routines: opening his shop early, measuring cloth, listening to the hum of traffic outside, and saving what he can because he has always believed that diligence is the surest way to keep life from unraveling. He lives alone and has long been used to doing things for himself. Friends describe him as quiet, respectful, and dependable, a man who takes pride in neat seams and finished hems. For years, his work gives him a sense of control and identity.

That changes on the day of the bombing. He is in a public place when the explosion happens, and in the first moments he does not understand what he is hearing. The sound is so loud and so sudden that it seems to split the air. He feels his body jerk before his mind catches up. In the chaos that follows, he sees people running, falling, shouting, and then he notices blood, dust, and pieces of what had once been ordinary life scattered everywhere. He remembers a smell of smoke mixed with something metallic and sickening. He does not know where to look or where to move, only that everything around him has become dangerous all at once.

Afterward, he spends days in a state of shock. He returns to work too soon, not because he feels ready, but because staying home leaves him alone with the images. At his tailoring table, his hands hover over fabric while his mind drifts back to the blast. He begins to notice that sudden noises make him flinch. A car backfiring, a dropped metal tray, even a customer slamming the shop door can send a wave through his chest and leave him breathless. He starts choosing where he sits in public so he can see entrances and exits. He no longer likes crowds, especially when people stand too close together. He tells himself he is simply being careful, but his body remains as if the danger has not passed.

At night, sleep becomes fragile. He lies awake replaying the scene in fragments: the sound, the smoke, the faces of strangers in fear. Sometimes he dreams that he is back there and cannot move his legs. Other times he wakes with his heart racing and his shirt damp with sweat, unsure whether he has heard an actual noise or only the memory of one. When he does sleep, it is light and broken. He becomes tired in a way that rest does not fix, and the tiredness follows him to the shop, where he makes small mistakes that would have embarrassed him before. He misses measurements, unpicks seams more than once, and finds himself staring at a finished sleeve without remembering when he last touched it.

He tries to keep busy, but he notices his mind avoiding anything that resembles the day of the attack. He changes the channel when news reports mention violence. He stops going to places that feel exposed, and he refuses invitations that would require him to travel far from home. He avoids talking about the bombing because once he starts, he fears he will not stop. Even when people ask simple questions about how he is doing, he answers quickly and moves the conversation elsewhere. The silence protects him, but it also leaves him feeling cut off from others. Being single has always suited his independence, yet now it deepens the sense that he is carrying something heavy alone.

Over time, he becomes more watchful and more easily startled. He scans surroundings automatically, measuring risk as if he is always on duty. His patience shortens. Minor frustrations at work — a late customer, a wrong order, a machine that jams — can leave him tense and irritable in a way that surprises him. He does not recognize himself in these moments and dislikes how quickly his temper rises. There are times when he feels detached, as if part of him is observing his own life from a distance while another part remains trapped in the aftermath of the explosion. He keeps going to work, keeps his shop open, keeps his face composed for others, but inside he feels narrowed by fear and memory.

Now, months later, he speaks of the attack as something that still lives in the room with him. He wants calm, yet calm feels unfamiliar and hard to trust. He continues to tailor clothes with careful hands, but the same precision that once gave him pride now coexists with vigilance, fatigue, and the constant effort of holding himself together through each day.
